Framework Evaluates Artificial Intelligence Outbreak Alerts Across Conflict-Affected Health Systems

A mini review evaluating infectious disease surveillance in conflict-affected health systems indicates that faster predictive performance from artificial intelligence does not necessarily translate into timely or equitable public health action. Writing in Frontiers in Public Health, researchers synthesized evidence on artificial intelligence early-warning tools alongside operational experiences from conventional humanitarian disease surveillance programmes to identify where alerting systems break down. The authors proposed a four-stage conceptual evaluation framework designed to assess data readiness, alert performance, verification and decision-making, and public health action and equity. The authors emphasize that direct empirical evidence linking artificial intelligence outbreak warnings to improved clinical or health outcomes in crisis settings remains limited, meaning early predictive detection cannot be treated as an established causal driver of reduced morbidity or mortality.

Surveillance in fragile and conflict-affected environments faces severe structural obstacles that undermine both the generation of reliable algorithmic predictions and the execution of response measures. Insecurity, damaged communications infrastructure, displaced populations, disrupted laboratory services, and critical health workforce shortages frequently disrupt routine data collection. The review highlights contextual findings from Southwest Cameroon, where routine integrated disease surveillance and response systems achieved timely reporting for cholera in only 16.3 percent of instances during intense conflict, compared to 40.7 percent during periods of reduced conflict intensity. In Borno State, Nigeria, a conventional Early Warning, Alert and Response System produced 13,737 alerts, yet only 16 required an immediate operational response after verification. Documented experiences from Yemen similarly demonstrate persistent diagnostic, transport, and governance hurdles that constrain outbreak verification during acute humanitarian emergencies.

The review formalizes these operational realities by organizing evaluation into four interconnected stages. Stage one focuses on data readiness, which examines whether surveillance inputs are sufficiently timely, complete, representative, and geographically informative before models ingest them. The researchers differentiate between reporting delays and data completeness, noting that an empty surveillance registry entry can signify absent disease, an unsubmitted report, a non-operational medical facility, or a severed communications link. In Sudan, conflict-related disruptions to malaria reporting created difficulties in interpreting longitudinal disease indicators because facility registries were outdated. Similarly, evaluations of Somalia’s electronic Early Warning and Response Network demonstrated continuous reporting challenges, showing that failing to account for missingness risks training models that identify shifts in reporting logistics rather than genuine changes in transmission dynamics.

Representativeness and population visibility constitute a critical component of the data readiness assessment. In crisis zones, displaced communities, informal settlement residents, and populations residing outside formal healthcare catchment areas often remain invisible to facility-based data streams. Research across Ugandan refugee settlements and broader refugee surveillance networks revealed parallel databases, fragmented reporting streams, and substantial coverage gaps, while findings from Lebanon showed difficulties in tracking refugee health when national registries do not disaggregate vulnerable cohorts. The review notes that an artificial intelligence model may produce swift, confident alerts for well-resourced, densely monitored populations while generating weak or absent signals for marginalized groups. Because algorithmic models reflect their training distributions, evaluation frameworks must quantify geographic and demographic coverage to detect systematic spatial and social blind spots.

Stage two of the framework evaluates alert performance using information available strictly at the time of prediction. The authors stress that assessing models retrospectively on finalized, cleaned datasets artificially inflates performance metrics, obscuring the operational reality of provisional, delayed, and noisy incoming data. Key evaluation indicators include sensitivity, positive predictive value, specificity, calibration, false-alert burden, and warning lead time against prespecified reference standards. The review cites an evaluation of a temporal data augmentation approach for outbreak detection in humanitarian settings that demonstrated a sensitivity of 0.72 alongside an annual false-alert burden of approximately 2.8 to 3.6 false alerts per local government area across temporal folds, illustrating the necessity of establishing baseline false-alarm rates before field deployment.

Stage three addresses verification and administrative decision-making, distinguishing an automated alert from a verified epidemiological event. Because alerts frequently require field investigation, contact tracing, and laboratory confirmation, an algorithm’s public health utility depends directly on how health authorities review incoming signals. In the conventional Borno State surveillance deployment, 89.6 percent of the 13,737 generated alerts were verified within 24 hours; subsequent investigations led to 9,794 alerts being discarded, 2,501 placed under monitoring, and exactly 16 prompting an active response. The researchers argue that evaluations must systematically track verification time, documentation of rationales, and the availability of diagnostic testing, ensuring that resources are not consumed by false-alarm investigations that overwhelm local clinical teams.

Stage four evaluates public health action and equity, focusing on whether verified signals trigger timely, proportionate, and equitable interventions. In fragile health systems, resource shortages frequently decouple verified outbreak detection from field response. Deficits in trained medical personnel, transport infrastructure, protective supplies, and physical security can prevent public health teams from reaching affected areas even when an alert is accurate. Indicators at this stage include the elapsed time from verification to response initiation, the overall geographic reach of interventions, and whether responses address underserved or displaced groups. The review cautions that unequal distribution of logistical resources can cause well-served populations to receive rapid outbreak containment while remote or displaced groups face unmitigated transmission despite equal or greater biological need.

The authors outline several methodological priorities for future research to bridge the gap between technical prediction and public health impact. Shadow-mode prospective evaluations, where model predictions run in parallel with existing surveillance workflows without directing operational resources, are recommended to quantify real-time predictive value without exposing fragile systems to unverified automated triggers. Furthermore, researchers must evaluate data management techniques such as nowcasting, missingness imputation, uncertainty-aware alert thresholds, and abstention strategies under live operational constraints. Implementation research must also investigate governance structures, clear chains of accountability, human oversight, and whether complex machine-learning algorithms offer verifiable operational advantages over simpler hybrid models combining standard indicators with local knowledge.

A primary limitation of the mini review is its focused narrative scope, which did not attempt an exhaustive systematic assessment across all existing surveillance literature. Furt
